---
title: "Binary outcomes"
subtitle: "Proportions, linear probability models and logistic regression"
bibliography: [../references.bib, ../references-new.bib]
---



The claim of the Housing and racial bias case study rests on a yes-or-no outcome, whether a housing authority's reply opened with the name of the person who had written to it. This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) fits to that outcome the models used in the course for outcomes of this kind. The original authors, whose field experiment is described on the [background page](../background.qmd), emailed public housing authorities from six names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic applicant [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. Starting from a table of counts, the module builds up to the logistic regression reported in the paper, allowing each step to be checked against the one before it. Every number is computed from the course files in `data/` when the page is built, with its code shown, while the course estimator, `fit_spec()` in `R/_tools.R`, performs the same arithmetic for every specification on the curve.

## 1. A yes-or-no outcome {#sec-outcome}

As a reply either opened with the sender's name or did not, the outcome takes the values 1 and 0, its mean in a group of replies thus corresponding to the share of replies that opened with the name. Every model on this page describes that share, the probability of a 1, and the way in which it differs between emails with Hispanic and with white names. The rows analysed are the replies to those two groups of names that carry a greeting code, selected by `spec_frame()` from the course estimator, with the outcome stored as `y` and the Hispanic names coded 1 in `hisp`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
frame <- spec_frame(housing, comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop")
counts <- table(hispanic = frame$hisp, named = frame$y)
counts
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
        named
hispanic   0   1
       0  68 107
       1 110  77
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
shares <- frame |> dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(), named = sum(y), share = mean(y), .by = hisp) |> dplyr::arrange(hisp)
shares
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 2 × 4
   hisp     n named share
  <int> <int> <dbl> <dbl>
1     0   175   107 0.611
2     1   187    77 0.412
```


:::
:::


Of the 175 coded replies to white names, 107 opened with the name, 61.1%, against 77 of the 187 replies to Hispanic names, 41.2%. Everything that follows describes, in one way or another, the difference between these two shares and the extent to which it could have arisen by chance.

## 2. The difference in proportions {#sec-difference}

The plainest summary is the difference between the two shares, −19.97 percentage points, which is also the scale on which the published abstract states the claim. Its standard error follows from the variance of a 0/1 variable, $p(1 - p)$ for a share $p$, each group contributing its own variance divided by its size.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
p1 <- shares$share[2]
p0 <- shares$share[1]
n1 <- shares$n[2]
n0 <- shares$n[1]
gap <- p1 - p0
se_gap <- sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1) / n1 + p0 * (1 - p0) / n0)
round(100 * c(gap = gap, se = se_gap, lower = gap - 1.96 * se_gap, upper = gap + 1.96 * se_gap), 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   gap     se  lower  upper 
-19.97   5.15 -30.06  -9.87 
```


:::
:::


The gap of −19.97 points has a standard error of 5.15 points and a 95% confidence interval from −30.1 to −9.9.

The classical test of the same difference is the $\chi^2$ test of the two-by-two table, available in R as `chisq.test()` and, in the form of a test of two proportions, as `prop.test()`. Both functions compare the observed counts with the counts expected if the two groups shared a single share of named greetings. Without a correction, the $\chi^2$ statistic is exactly the square of the z obtained for the two proportions when that shared share enters its standard error.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pooled <- mean(frame$y)
z_pooled <- gap / sqrt(pooled * (1 - pooled) * (1 / n1 + 1 / n0))
c(z_squared = z_pooled^2,
  chisq_uncorrected = unname(chisq.test(counts, correct = FALSE)$statistic),
  chisq_corrected = unname(chisq.test(counts)$statistic),
  prop_test = unname(prop.test(counts[, 2:1])$statistic)) |>
  round(3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
        z_squared chisq_uncorrected   chisq_corrected         prop_test 
           14.419            14.419            13.632            13.632 
```


:::
:::


The last two numbers differ from the first two because `chisq.test()` and `prop.test()` apply the continuity correction to a two-by-two table unless they are told otherwise. The correction, due to Yates, shrinks each difference between an observed and an expected count by half a unit before it is squared, which makes the test a little more conservative, and it bears on the reproduction in Task 3. Analyst 8PTRZ compared the Hispanic names with all other names among the replies and recorded $\chi^2$ = 14.265, the corrected value, while analyst 25N5D recorded the corrected `prop.test()` statistic of 13.683 for the comparison among all delivered emails.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
frame_8ptrz <- spec_frame(housing, comparison = "nonhispanic", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop")
frame_25n5d <- spec_frame(housing, comparison = "white", population = "all", uncoded = "not_named")
tab_8ptrz <- table(frame_8ptrz$hisp, frame_8ptrz$y)
c(`8PTRZ` = unname(chisq.test(tab_8ptrz)$statistic),
  `8PTRZ, uncorrected` = unname(chisq.test(tab_8ptrz, correct = FALSE)$statistic),
  `25N5D` = unname(prop.test(table(frame_25n5d$hisp, frame_25n5d$y)[, 2:1])$statistic)) |>
  round(3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
             8PTRZ 8PTRZ, uncorrected              25N5D 
            14.265             14.952             13.683 
```


:::
:::


Both recorded values are reproduced exactly, and without the correction the statistic recorded by 8PTRZ would have been 14.95. A reproduction depends on the software defaults as well as on the data and the model. On the specification curve the test of a table serves as a check, every specification being tested by its model instead, because a model can include covariates and a table cannot.

## 3. The linear probability model {#sec-lpm}

A linear regression of the 0/1 outcome on the 0/1 indicator of the Hispanic names is known as a linear probability model. With a single binary predictor it reproduces the table exactly, its intercept being the share among the white names and its coefficient the difference in proportions.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lpm <- lm(y ~ hisp, data = frame)
round(coef(lpm), 4)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
(Intercept)        hisp 
     0.6114     -0.1997 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# classical errors; HC2 errors (MacKinnon and White 1985) from the sandwich
# package (Zeileis 2004, Journal of Statistical Software); and the standard
# error of the difference between two means computed group by group, from the
# Welch t-test
se <- c(classical = sqrt(vcov(lpm)["hisp", "hisp"]),
        hc2 = sqrt(sandwich::vcovHC(lpm, type = "HC2")["hisp", "hisp"]),
        two_sample = t.test(y ~ hisp, data = frame)$stderr)
round(100 * se, 4)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 classical        hc2 two_sample 
    5.1666     5.1649     5.1649 
```


:::
:::


The classical formula for the standard error of a linear regression assumes that the outcome varies equally in both groups, which a 0/1 outcome cannot do unless the two shares are equal or add up to one, given that its variance is $p(1 - p)$. The HC2 standard error, one of the heteroskedasticity-consistent errors that allow the variance to differ between observations, drops that assumption, and with one binary predictor it equals the standard error of a difference between two means computed group by group, the formula used for comparing two randomised groups. The course computes it with `vcovHC()` from the sandwich package, reached by the course estimator through `parameters::model_parameters(lpm, vcov = "HC2")`, and the `estimatr` package yields the same number with `lm_robust(y ~ hisp, se_type = "HC2")`. Here the classical and the HC2 errors differ by only 0.002 points, because the two groups are of similar size and the two shares not far apart, but the HC2 error is the one that remains correct when these conditions do not hold.

The linear probability model has a well-known fault, which becomes apparent once covariates enter the model, in that a straight line has no floor or ceiling and can thus predict a share below 0 or above 1. With the covariates used on the curve, which comprise a handful of categories, the predictions remain well inside that range on these data.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lpm_adjusted <- lm(y ~ hisp + hard_email + pop_third + poverty_third + black_third + hispanic_third,
                   data = frame)
round(range(fitted(lpm_adjusted)), 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.213 0.792
```


:::
:::


In an experiment with a binary treatment, the linear probability model has a second virtue, in that its coefficient is the difference in proportions, the quantity named by the claim, whether or not covariates are added. On this curve the covariates shift that coefficient by less than the width of its standard error, which is why the reference specification is a linear probability model without covariates.

## 4. Logistic regression {#sec-logit}

The model reported in the paper is a logistic regression, which models the log of the odds of a greeting, $\log(p / (1 - p))$. This transformation of the share ranges over the whole real line and thus keeps every prediction between 0 and 1, the coefficients of the model being differences in log odds.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
logit <- glm(y ~ hisp, family = binomial(), data = frame)
round(coef(logit), 4)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
(Intercept)        hisp 
     0.4533     -0.8100 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
round(exp(coef(logit)[["hisp"]]), 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.445
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
predicted <- predict(logit, newdata = tibble::tibble(hisp = c(0, 1)), type = "response")
round(100 * predicted, 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
    1     2 
61.14 41.18 
```


:::
:::


The coefficient of the Hispanic names is −0.810, close to the −0.82 reported in the paper, whose model also included the community covariates and the hard-to-find address and fitted all three groups of names at once. Exponentiated, this coefficient corresponds to an odds ratio of 0.445, meaning that the odds that a reply to a Hispanic name opened with the name were 0.44 times the odds for a white name. Without covariates the model reproduces the two observed shares exactly, 61.1% and 41.2%, and the difference between these shares is thus again the gap of −19.97 points.

The original authors fitted the three groups in one model, as did the analysts EWFMI and P9W8Y. The original authors took the white names as the base category and EWFMI the Hispanic names, which is why the z reported by that analyst is positive, while P9W8Y reported an omnibus test, which does not depend on the base. Without covariates, the three-group model yields exactly the same coefficient for the Hispanic names as the two-group model, since each coefficient compares one group with the base and the third group adds nothing to that comparison.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
three <- housing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(reply == 1, !is.na(named)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(group = relevel(factor(group), ref = "white"))
round(coef(glm(named ~ group, family = binomial(), data = three)), 4)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  (Intercept)    groupblack grouphispanic 
       0.4533       -0.2072       -0.8100 
```


:::
:::


With covariates the two models differ a little, because the emails with Black names then contribute to the estimation of the covariates, and the specification menu retains the three-group model as a check on the two-group fit.

## 5. Odds ratios and percentage points {#sec-scales}

Odds ratios are the conventional way of reporting a logistic regression, and while they are exact and portable, they are hard to picture, because the same odds ratio corresponds to very different changes in probability at different starting points. The chunk below applies the odds ratio estimated from the data to four shares of named greetings for the white names.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
odds_ratio <- exp(coef(logit)[["hisp"]])
base <- c(0.20, 0.50, 0.61, 0.90)
odds_hisp <- odds_ratio * base / (1 - base)
or_gaps <- 100 * (odds_hisp / (1 + odds_hisp) - base)
round(or_gaps, 1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] -10.0 -19.2 -20.0 -10.0
```


:::
:::


The odds ratio of 0.445 turns a share of 61% into a gap of −20.0 points, but a share of 20% into a gap of −10.0 points and a share of 90% into one of −10.0.

The claim, as stated in the abstract, gives the gap in percentage points, as does every point of the curve. A logistic regression reports its result on that scale through an average marginal effect, the difference in the predicted probability of a greeting between a Hispanic and a white name, computed for every analysed email as it stands and then averaged. The course estimator computes it with `avg_comparisons()` from the marginaleffects package, which sets the indicator of the Hispanic names to 1 and then to 0 in every row, predicts the probability of a greeting each time and averages the difference, while `avg_predictions()` shows the two averages from which the difference is taken. A detail that catches users of the package out is its refusal of a data column called `group`, which is why the model is fitted on the model columns alone.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
model_cols <- frame |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("y", "hisp", "hard_email", "pop_third", "poverty_third", "black_third", "hispanic_third")) |>
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::if_all(dplyr::everything(), \(x) !is.na(x)))
logit_adjusted <- glm(y ~ hisp + hard_email + pop_third + poverty_third + black_third + hispanic_third,
                      family = binomial(), data = model_cols)
# the average predicted probability with every email signed by a white name and
# by a Hispanic one, and their difference with its delta-method standard error
marginaleffects::avg_predictions(logit_adjusted, variables = list(hisp = 0:1))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

 hisp Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)     S 2.5 % 97.5 %
    0    0.602     0.0368 16.4   <0.001 197.5 0.530  0.674
    1    0.422     0.0361 11.7   <0.001 102.7 0.352  0.493

Type: response
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ame <- marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(logit_adjusted, variables = "hisp")
round(100 * c(ame = ame$estimate, se = ame$std.error), 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
    ame      se 
-17.984   5.184 
```


:::
:::


The difference between the two average predictions is the average marginal effect, and across the 32 logistic specifications of the curve the odds ratio ranges from 0.443 to 0.533 and the average marginal effect from −20.0 to −12.2 points. A related rule bounds the size of a logistic coefficient on the probability scale. As the slope of the logistic curve is steepest, at one quarter, where the probability is one half, a coefficient $b$ shifts a probability by at most $b/4$. The coefficient of 0.098 found by the replication of the paper in the SCORE replicability study for its Hispanic names therefore corresponds to a gap of at most 2.45 points, in favour of the Hispanic names.

## 6. Odds ratios and covariates {#sec-collapsibility}

In a randomised experiment, adding a covariate that predicts the outcome does not change what a difference in proportions estimates, because the covariate is unrelated to the treatment, whereas it does change what an odds ratio estimates, even with no confounding at all. The odds ratio is said to be non-collapsible, meaning that an odds ratio which holds within each group of a covariate does not hold for the groups taken together, as the following arithmetic shows. Suppose the authorities were of two kinds, equally many of each, and that white names were greeted by name 85% of the time by one kind and 35% of the time by the other, which averages to about the 61% observed in the data. Let the Hispanic names multiply the odds of a greeting, in both kinds of authority, by the odds ratio estimated from the data.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
white_by_kind <- c(0.85, 0.35)
hisp_odds <- odds_ratio * white_by_kind / (1 - white_by_kind)
hisp_by_kind <- hisp_odds / (1 + hisp_odds)
white_all <- mean(white_by_kind)
hisp_all <- mean(hisp_by_kind)
round(c(or_within = odds_ratio,
        or_all = (hisp_all / (1 - hisp_all)) / (white_all / (1 - white_all)),
        gap_kind_1 = 100 * (hisp_by_kind[1] - white_by_kind[1]),
        gap_kind_2 = 100 * (hisp_by_kind[2] - white_by_kind[2]),
        gap_all = 100 * (hisp_all - white_all)), 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 or_within     or_all gap_kind_1 gap_kind_2    gap_all 
     0.445      0.556    -13.402    -15.675    -14.539 
```


:::
:::


Within each kind of authority the odds ratio is 0.445, but for all authorities together it is 0.556, closer to 1, although nothing is confounded and the names were assigned at random. The gaps in percentage points behave as one would hope, the gap for all authorities, −14.5 points, being the average of the gaps within the two kinds. A logistic regression that adjusts for the kind of authority would report an odds ratio of 0.445, and one that does not would report 0.556, both being right about different quantities, namely the odds ratio within a kind of authority and the odds ratio over all authorities.

Since the covariates predict the greeting only weakly in the Housing data, the effect is small and mixes with the chance differences between the groups. On the 357 replies that carry every covariate, the adjusted model yields an odds ratio of 0.470 against 0.456 without covariates, and an average marginal effect of −18.0 against −19.4 points. Both shifts appear to come mainly from small imbalances in the covariates between the groups, which adjustment corrects, rather than from non-collapsibility. The principle matters, however, whenever the results of different analyses are compared. An odds ratio from a model with covariates and one from a model without them are not estimates of the same quantity. Two analysts who report odds ratios from different models can thus differ for that reason alone, which is one reason why the course reports every logistic specification as an average marginal effect in points.

## 7. The methods side by side {#sec-side-by-side}

Every method on this page can be applied to the single comparison made in the reference specification, Hispanic against white names among the 362 coded replies, and @tbl-side-by-side brings the results together in one table.


::: {#tbl-side-by-side .cell tbl-cap='One comparison, Hispanic against white names among the coded replies, reported by each method of the page: the estimate on its own scale, its standard error, the test statistic and the two-sided p-value. The randomisation p-value is stored in the curve file. Sources: `data/housing_emails.csv`, `data/spec_curve.csv`.'}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
# each model reported by parameters (classical, HC2 and Wald z), the average
# marginal effect by marginaleffects
lpm_classical <- parameters::model_parameters(lpm) |> datawizard::data_filter(Parameter == "hisp")
lpm_hc2 <- parameters::model_parameters(lpm, vcov = "HC2") |> datawizard::data_filter(Parameter == "hisp")
logit_row <- parameters::model_parameters(logit) |> datawizard::data_filter(Parameter == "hisp")
logit_z <- logit_row$z
# marginaleffects refuses a data column called group, so the logit is refitted
# on the model columns alone for it
logit_ame <- glm(y ~ hisp, family = binomial(),
                 data = datawizard::data_select(frame, select = c("y", "hisp"))) |>
  marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(variables = "hisp")
chi_plain <- chisq.test(counts, correct = FALSE)
chi_yates <- chisq.test(counts)
ref_spec <- curve |> datawizard::data_filter(is_reference)
all_p <- c(2 * pnorm(-abs(gap / se_gap)), chi_plain$p.value, chi_yates$p.value,
           lpm_hc2$p, logit_row$p, ref_spec$p_ri)
tibble::tribble(
  ~Method, ~Estimate, ~SE, ~Statistic, ~p,
  "Difference in proportions", fmt(100 * gap, 2), fmt(100 * se_gap, 2),
    paste("z =", fmt(gap / se_gap, 2)), pe(2 * pnorm(-abs(gap / se_gap))),
  "χ<sup>2</sup> test, uncorrected", "", "", paste("χ<sup>2</sup> =", fmt(chi_plain$statistic, 2)),
    pe(chi_plain$p.value),
  "χ<sup>2</sup> test, with the continuity correction", "", "",
    paste("χ<sup>2</sup> =", fmt(chi_yates$statistic, 2)), pe(chi_yates$p.value),
  "Linear probability model, classical errors", fmt(100 * lpm_classical$Coefficient, 2),
    fmt(100 * lpm_classical$SE, 2), paste("t =", fmt(lpm_classical$t, 2)), pe(lpm_classical$p),
  "Linear probability model, HC2 errors", fmt(100 * lpm_hc2$Coefficient, 2),
    fmt(100 * lpm_hc2$SE, 2), paste("t =", fmt(lpm_hc2$t, 2)), pe(lpm_hc2$p),
  "Logistic regression, coefficient", fmt(logit_row$Coefficient, 3), fmt(logit_row$SE, 3),
    paste("z =", fmt(logit_z, 3)), pe(logit_row$p),
  "Logistic regression, average marginal effect", fmt(100 * logit_ame$estimate, 2),
    fmt(100 * logit_ame$std.error, 2), "", "",
  "Randomisation test", "", "", "", paste("p =", fmt(ref_spec$p_ri, 4))
) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:5, align = "r")
```

Every method finds the same gap, or a statistic that tests it, and the largest p-value in the table is 0.0005, that of the randomisation test, which cannot go lower with 1,999 reshuffles. The z of the logistic coefficient, −3.771, is the value recorded by analyst UYV3F. The methods differ in what they can include and in the scale on which they report, a table test including no covariates, a linear probability model reporting in points and a logistic regression in log odds unless it is converted. The methods also differ in the statistic that they pass on to anyone who converts results to a common scale, which is why the same gap became different correlations in the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], as the [background page](../background.qmd#sec-scale) shows.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Change the two shares of the arithmetic in section 6 to 0.65 and 0.55, which predict the greeting much more weakly, and rerun the chunk. How far does the odds ratio for all authorities now move from the odds ratio within them? Then go back to 0.85 and 0.35 and replace the odds ratio of the data with 1, the case where the names make no difference: does the odds ratio for all authorities still move?
:::

## 8. Where this leads {#sec-next}

The specification curve takes the models of sections 1 to 7 as they stand, and the [specification menu](../menu.qmd) explains which of these models are retained on the curve. The simulations in the [experiments module](experiments.qmd#sec-simulation) use the difference in proportions with HC2 errors as the estimator of a simulated experiment, showing what the estimator recovers when the name changes only the greeting and what it misses when the name also changes who replies, while the [multiverse module](multiverse.qmd) examines the specification curve as a whole.

## Sources {#sec-sources}

The models on this page are fitted with `lm()` and `glm()` from base R, with the HC2 standard error and the average marginal effect taken from the course estimator in `R/_tools.R`, which is checked by `R/check_parity.R` against `estimatr` and `marginaleffects`. The data are in `data/housing_emails.csv` and the curve in `data/spec_curve.csv`, both with codebooks, while the analyses reported by the five analysts in the robustness study are in `analysts5.csv`. @GelmanEtAl2020RegressionOtherStories treat logistic regression and its interpretation on the probability scale at length, and the [specification menu](../menu.qmd#level-estimation) explains which models, tests and scales are retained on the specification curve.
